docs.title: lvm_tools Documentation
docs.text:
lvm_tools is a lightweight, modular wrapper for the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Local Volume Mapper (LVM) Data Reduction Pipeline (DRP) products. The package provides efficient, lazy data loading via Dask, making it suitable for large-scale spectroscopic analysis and model fitting.

The package is designed for use with spectrospatial models via spectracles, though its modular architecture supports a variety of downstream applications.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Lazy data loading: Read LVM DRP FITS files using Dask for memory-efficient processing of large datasets
  • Modular data configuration: Flexible configuration system for wavelength clipping, spatial filtering, and data normalisation
  • Reproducible pipelines: Hash-based tracking of data processing configurations for reproducibility
  • JAX integration: Seamless conversion to JAX arrays for GPU-accelerated model fitting
  • xarray-based storage: Data stored in xarray Datasets for intuitive, labelled array manipulation

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The recommended installation method is via PyPI:

pip install lvm-tools

Alternatively, using uv (recommended):

uv add lvm-tools

For development, clone and install from source:

git clone git@github.com:TomHilder/lvm_tools.git
cd lvm_tools
pip install -e .

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from lvm_tools import LVMTile, DataConfig, FitDataBuilder

# Load a single tile from a DRP file
tile = LVMTile.from_file(Path("path/to/lvm-drp-file.fits"))

# Create a configuration for data processing
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    tile,
    λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0),  # Wavelength range in Angstroms
)

# Build fit-ready data
fit_data = FitDataBuilder(tile, config).build()

# Access normalised arrays for model fitting
flux = fit_data.flux  # Normalised flux (JAX array)
wavelength = fit_data.λ  # Wavelength grid (JAX array)

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to lvm_tools are documented in this file.

The format follows Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Sky positions in arcseconds, for spectracles models with physical length scales: FitData.sky_x and FitData.sky_y are each spaxel's offset east and north of a centre, on the tangent plane (astropy's SkyOffsetFrame, so the cos δ factor is exact across the field), and FitData.sky_data is a SpatialDataLVM with them.
  • FitData.sky_centre: the (RA, Dec) the offsets are measured from, by default the centre of the spaxels' bounding box (correct across RA = 0). FitData.with_sky_origin(ra, dec) sets it, e.g. to put several datasets on one frame.

  • FitData.sky_to_radec(x, y): offsets back to RA and Dec, e.g. for maps on a grid.

  • Tests (tests/), run in CI on Python 3.10 to 3.14.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• F_range's upper bound was ignored for single pixels: with F_bad_strategy="pixel" (and in filter_inspector), flux above the upper bound wasn't excluded. Only fits with a finite upper bound are affected; the default is infinite.
  • DataConfig now rejects exclusion strategies that filtering doesn't support (None for either setting, "spaxel_max" for nans_strategy) when it is created, instead of the build failing later.
  • Type annotations of LVMTile.get_metadata, LVMTileMeta.tile_id (an int or a string) and the normalisation helpers now match what they return; get_norm_funcs returns a tuple rather than a one-use generator.

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text:
• The coordinates scaled into [-π, π]: FitData.α, FitData.δ, FitData.αδ_data, FitData.predict_α, FitData.predict_δ and FitData.arcsec_to_model_domain warn (DeprecationWarning) and will be removed in a future release. Use sky_x, sky_y, sky_data and sky_to_radec, with a spectracles Domain for physical length scales. They still return the same values.

DataConfig and FitDataBuilder.hash() are unchanged, so existing hashes are too. The sky origin (with_sky_origin) is a choice of frame, not part of the data, and isn't included in the hash.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The spectracles extra now requires spectracles 1.0 or later, which has the Domain that arcsec positions (sky_data) need for physical length scales.
  • The documentation is now built with MkDocs Material (as spectracles' is), from Markdown in docs/. The content is unchanged.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• FitDataBuilder.hash() crashed when given a single LVMTile (it only worked for collections). Hashes for collections are unchanged.
  • Clipping or filtering away all the data now raises a ValueError that names the ranges, instead of an obscure TypeError from the normalisation.
  • Documentation: code examples that failed on real data, stale descriptions of the "padded" and "Nσ" normalisations, and dependency minimums that didn't match the package.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Invalid normalisation offsets or scales (NaN, infinite, or a non-positive scale) raise ValueError instead of a bare Exception. Code that caught Exception still catches them.
  • The spectracles extra now installs spectracles on Python 3.11 and later (matching spectracles' own requirement), instead of only on 3.13 and later.
  • Development: ruff is in the dev dependency group, and CI runs ruff check and ruff format --check.
  • Documentation moved from ReadTheDocs to GitHub Pages (https://tomhilder.github.io/lvm_tools/), deployed with each release.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • LVMTile.from_file no longer reads whole cubes. Each cube is now chunked along wavelength and only the chunks in the selected wavelength range are read and byte-swapped. For an Hα window over 49 Rosette frames, loading went from 7.9 s and 16 GB to 0.5 s and 3.7 GB, with bit-identical output.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • NORM_PADDING increased from 0.01 to 0.15. The "padded" normalisation maps the data onto the periodic domain of the Fourier-basis GP, and 1% padding let the field wrap onto itself across the domain edge. This changes the output of every "padded" normalisation, so fitted coordinates and arcsec_to_model_domain results shift.
Initial release.

docs.title: Configuration API
docs.text:
DataConfig holds every setting for preparing data for fitting: which wavelengths and sky region to keep, which data to exclude, and how to normalise the flux and coordinates. It is exported from the top-level lvm_tools namespace.

from lvm_tools import DataConfig

config = DataConfig.from_tiles(tile, λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0))  # computed from the data
config = DataConfig.default()  # all defaults
d = config.to_dict()
config = DataConfig.from_dict(d)

docs.title: lvm_tools.DataConfig dataclass
docs.text:
Settings for preparing LVM data for fitting: what to select, what to exclude, and how to normalise it.

A DataConfig is immutable. Usually it is made with DataConfig.from_tiles, which works out the RA/Dec ranges and the normalisation offsets and scales from the data, and then passed with the tiles to FitDataBuilder.

The strategies, F_range, fibre_status_include, apply_mask and the normalisation offsets and scales are checked when the config is created, raising ValueError (or TypeError for a value of the wrong type). The wavelength, RA and Dec ranges are checked when the data are clipped.

Attributes:

Name Type Description λ_range Range | Ranges

Wavelength range(s) to keep, in Angstrom. A single range (min, max), or several ranges ((min1, max1), (min2, max2), ...) in increasing order and not overlapping, whose selections are joined along wavelength. Each range needs min < max. Default (-inf, inf).

α_range Range

Right ascension range (min, max) to keep, in degrees. Default (-inf, inf).

δ_range Range

Declination range (min, max) to keep, in degrees. Default (-inf, inf).

nans_strategy ExcludeStrategy

How to exclude NaN fluxes. "pixel" leaves them as individual NaN pixels; "spaxel" excludes every spaxel with any NaN flux. Default "pixel".

F_bad_strategy ExcludeStrategy

How to exclude bad fluxes using F_range. "pixel" excludes each pixel whose flux is at or below F_range[0] or above F_range[1]; "spaxel" excludes spaxels whose median flux over wavelength is outside F_range; "spaxel_max" excludes spaxels whose maximum flux is outside F_range. Both spaxel strategies also exclude spaxels whose fluxes are all NaN. Default "spaxel".

F_range Range

Range (min, max) of acceptable flux, in erg cm⁻² s⁻¹ Å⁻¹, used by F_bad_strategy. Default (BAD_FLUX_THRESHOLD, inf), i.e. (-1e-14, inf).

fibre_status_include tuple[FibreStatus]

Fibre status values to keep (each 0, 1, 2 or 3); spaxels with any other status are excluded. Default (0,).

apply_mask bool

Whether to exclude the pixels flagged in the DRP mask. Default True.

normalise_F_strategy NormaliseStrategy

How from_tiles computes the flux normalisation (see NormaliseStrategy and calc_normalisation). Default "max only".

normalise_F_offset float

Offset of the flux normalisation; the normalised flux is (flux - offset) / scale. Must be a finite float. Default 0.0.

normalise_F_scale float

Scale of the flux normalisation. Must be a positive, finite float. The inverse variance is multiplied by scale**2. Default 1.0.

normalise_αδ_strategy NormaliseStrategy

How from_tiles computes the RA and Dec normalisations (same options as normalise_F_strategy). Default "padded".

normalise_α_offset float

Offset of the RA normalisation, in degrees. Default 0.0.

normalise_α_scale float

Scale of the RA normalisation, in degrees. Default 1.0.

normalise_δ_offset float

Offset of the Dec normalisation, in degrees. Default 0.0.

normalise_δ_scale float

Scale of the Dec normalisation, in degrees. Default 1.0.

Example 
from lvm_tools import DataConfig

config = DataConfig.from_tiles(tile, λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0))
config = DataConfig.from_dict(config.to_dict() | {"apply_mask": False})

docs.title: from_tiles(tiles, λ_range=(-np.inf, np.inf), **overrides) staticmethod
docs.text:
A config with the RA/Dec ranges and normalisations computed from the data.

The steps are:

  1. Set α_range and δ_range to a square around all the spaxels of tiles (see get_αδ_ranges).
  2. Clip and filter the data with that config, λ_range and any overrides.
  3. Compute the flux, RA and Dec normalisations of what is left, using the normalisation strategies. RA and Dec get the larger of their two scales, so the normalised coordinates keep the sky's aspect ratio.
  4. Apply overrides again, so they take precedence over the computed values.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default tiles LVMTileLike

The data to configure for.

required λ_range Range | Ranges

Wavelength range(s) to keep, in Angstrom (see the λ_range attribute). It is not computed from the data.

(-inf, inf) **overrides Any

Any other attributes, by name, e.g. nans_strategy="spaxel".

{}

Returns:

Type Description DataConfig

The config.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If an override is not an attribute of DataConfig, if a setting is invalid, or if no data are left after clipping or filtering.

TypeError

If a setting has the wrong type.

Example 
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    tile,
    λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0),
    normalise_F_strategy="98 only",
)

docs.title: Fit Data API
docs.text:
FitDataBuilder turns tiles and a DataConfig into FitData: normalised, model-ready JAX arrays with sky positions and indices. FitDataBuilder is exported from the top-level lvm_tools namespace; FitData lives in lvm_tools.fit_data.fit_data.

import jax.numpy as jnp
from lvm_tools import DataConfig, FitDataBuilder, LVMTile

tile = LVMTile.from_file("/data/observation.fits")
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(tile, λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0))
fit_data = FitDataBuilder(tiles=tile, config=config).build()

# Spectra have shape (n_wavelengths, n_spaxels); average over the spaxels with data
weights = fit_data.mask.astype(jnp.float32)
mean_flux = jnp.sum(fit_data.flux * weights, axis=1) / jnp.sum(weights, axis=1)

# Spaxel positions in arcsec east and north of fit_data.sky_centre, and back to RA, Dec
x, y = fit_data.sky_x, fit_data.sky_y
ra, dec = fit_data.sky_to_radec(x, y)

print(f"Mean barycentric velocity: {float(fit_data.v_bary.mean()):.2f} km/s")

docs.text:
Builds FitData from tiles and a config, and identifies the pair by a hash.

Attributes:

Name Type Description tiles LVMTileLike

The data: one tile or a collection.

config DataConfig

The processing config, usually from DataConfig.from_tiles on the same tiles.

Example 
from lvm_tools import DataConfig, FitDataBuilder, LVMTile

tile = LVMTile.from_file(path)
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(tile, λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0))

builder = FitDataBuilder(tiles=tile, config=config)
fit_data = builder.build()

docs.title: build()
docs.text:
Process the tiles with the config and package the result for fitting.

The steps are:

  1. Clip the data to the config's wavelength, RA and Dec ranges.
  2. Set the data the config excludes to NaN (NaNs, bad flux, fibre status, mask).
  3. Flatten the tile and spaxel dimensions into one spaxel dimension.
  4. Make the normalisation functions from the config's offsets and scales (the normalisation strategies are not applied again here).

Returns:

Type Description FitData

The data, ready for fitting.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If no data are left after clipping or filtering, or a strategy is not supported by the filtering.

docs.title: hash()
docs.text:
A SHA-256 hash identifying the config and the tiles.

It is computed from the config's attributes and each tile's metadata (filename, tile ID, exposure number and DRP version), both serialised as JSON with sorted keys. It identifies the inputs, not the data values.

Returns:

Type Description str

The hash, as a hexadecimal string.

Example 
pipeline_hash = builder.hash()
print(f"Pipeline: {pipeline_hash[:16]}...")

docs.title: lvm_tools.fit_data.fit_data.FitData dataclass
docs.text:
LVM data ready for model fitting: normalised arrays, positions and indices as JAX arrays.

Usually made by FitDataBuilder.build. The data are held as a flattened xarray dataset plus the normalisation functions, and each property computes its JAX array from them when accessed.

The spectral arrays (flux, i_var, u_flux, lsf_σ, mask) have shape (n_wavelengths, n_spaxels), and the per-spaxel arrays (sky_x, sky_y, the indices, mjd, v_bary) have shape (n_spaxels,), where the spaxels of every tile are counted together. Floating-point arrays are 32-bit unless JAX's 64-bit mode is on. Pixels that were clipped or filtered out are NaN in the processed data; mask marks the others, and the spectral properties replace the NaNs with fill values so they can be used in a likelihood together with mask.

Sky positions are given as sky_x and sky_y: offsets in arcsec east and north of sky_centre, on the tangent plane. sky_data packages them for spectracles. The members that scale the coordinates into [-π, π] (α, δ, αδ_data, predict_α, predict_δ, arcsec_to_model_domain) are deprecated and emit DeprecationWarning.

Attributes:

Name Type Description processed_data Dataset

The clipped, filtered data, flattened to dimensions (wavelength, flat_spaxel) (see flatten_tile_coord).

normalise_flux Callable

Normalises a flux, (flux - offset) / scale.

predict_flux Callable

Turns a normalised flux back into erg cm⁻² s⁻¹ Å⁻¹.

normalise_ivar Callable

Normalises an inverse variance (multiplies it by the flux scale squared).

predict_ivar Callable

Turns a normalised inverse variance back into physical units.

normalise_α Callable

Normalises a right ascension in degrees.

normalise_δ Callable

Normalises a declination in degrees.

sky_origin tuple[float, float] | None

The (RA, Dec) in degrees to measure sky offsets from, or None (the default) for the centre of the spaxels' bounding box. Set it with with_sky_origin.

The fields are, in order: processed_data, normalise_flux, predict_flux, normalise_ivar, predict_ivar, normalise_α, the inverse of normalise_α, normalise_δ, the inverse of normalise_δ, and sky_origin.

Example 
fit_data = FitDataBuilder(tiles=tile, config=config).build()
x, y = fit_data.sky_x, fit_data.sky_y  # arcsec
flux, i_var, mask = fit_data.flux, fit_data.i_var, fit_data.mask

docs.title: Sky positions
docs.text: Positions are offsets in arcsec on the tangent plane at sky_centre.

docs.title: sky_x property
docs.text:
Each spaxel's offset east of sky_centre, in arcsec, shape (n_spaxels,).

The offsets are coordinates on the tangent plane at sky_centre (astropy's SkyOffsetFrame), so they include the cos(Dec) factor. They are computed in 64-bit precision before being converted to a JAX array.

docs.title: sky_y property
docs.text:
Each spaxel's offset north of sky_centre, in arcsec, shape (n_spaxels,).

Computed as for sky_x, on the tangent plane at sky_centre.

docs.title: sky_centre property
docs.text:
The (RA, Dec) in degrees that sky_x and sky_y are measured from.

This is sky_origin if set, otherwise the centre of the spaxels' bounding box in RA and Dec. The bounding box is found with RA measured relative to the first spaxel, so a footprint that crosses RA = 0 is handled.

required

docs.title: sky_data property
docs.text:
The spaxel positions for spectracles, as arcsec offsets from sky_centre.

A spectracles SpatialDataLVM with x = sky_x, y = sky_y, and the spaxel, tile, IFU and fibre indices (spaxel_idx, tile_idx, ifu_idx, fibre_idx). Length scales of spectracles fields are then in arcsec. Build the field's region with spectracles.Domain.from_points(d.x, d.y). Requires the optional spectracles dependency (pip install lvm_tools[spectracles]).

Raises:

Type Description ModuleNotFoundError

If spectracles could not be imported.

Example 
from spectracles import Domain

spaxels = fit_data.sky_data

docs.title: Spectral data
docs.text: Arrays of shape (n_wavelengths, n_spaxels), plus the wavelength grid.

docs.title: flux property
docs.text: Normalised flux, shape (n_wavelengths, n_spaxels), with NaNs (excluded pixels) set to 0.

docs.title: i_var property
docs.text: Normalised inverse variance of flux, shape (n_wavelengths, n_spaxels), with NaNs set to 1e-4.

docs.title: u_flux property
docs.text:
Normalised flux uncertainty, i_var**-0.5 (before its NaNs are filled), shape (n_wavelengths, n_spaxels), with NaNs set to 100.

Infinite values (where the inverse variance is 0) become the largest finite float, as in jax.numpy.nan_to_num.

docs.title: mask property
docs.text: Which pixels hold data, shape (n_wavelengths, n_spaxels): True where the flux is not NaN, i.e. the pixel survived clipping and filtering.

docs.title: λ property
docs.text: Wavelengths in Angstrom, shape (n_wavelengths,).

docs.title: lsf_σ property
docs.text: Gaussian standard deviation of the line spread function in Angstrom (not normalised), shape (n_wavelengths, n_spaxels), with NaNs set to the median of the rest.

docs.title: λ_idx property
docs.text: Wavelength indices 0 .. n_wavelengths - 1.

docs.title: spaxel_idx property
docs.text: Spaxel indices 0 .. n_spaxels - 1, counting the spaxels of every tile together.

docs.title: tile_idx property
docs.text: Index of each spaxel's tile, shape (n_spaxels,): the tiles' exposure numbers replaced by 0 .. n_tiles - 1, in increasing order of exposure number.

docs.title: ifu_idx property
docs.text: Index of each spaxel's IFU bundle, shape (n_spaxels,): the IFU labels replaced by 0 .. n_ifus - 1, in sorted order of label.

docs.title: fibre_idx property
docs.text: Fibre identifier of each spaxel, shape (n_spaxels,). These are the slitmap's fibre IDs, not re-indexed, so gaps from excluded fibres are kept.

docs.title: mjd property
docs.text: Modified Julian Date of the midpoint of each spaxel's exposure, shape (n_spaxels,).

docs.title: v_bary property
docs.text:
Barycentric velocity correction of each spaxel in km/s, shape (n_spaxels,).

Computed by get_v_barycentric for Las Campanas Observatory, at each spaxel's position and exposure midpoint.

docs.text:
Count how many pixels and spaxels each filter would exclude, to help choose a config.

Each entry of the result is a pair (n_pixels, n_spaxels), with None where a count doesn't apply:

  • "nans": NaN fluxes, and spaxels with any NaN flux.
  • "bad flux": pixels flagged by get_where_bad (the "pixel" strategy).
  • "bad flux median": spaxels flagged by get_where_bad_median (the "spaxel" strategy).
  • "fibre status": spaxels whose fibre status is not in fibre_status_include.
  • "mask": pixels flagged in the DRP mask, and spaxels with any flagged pixel.
  • "any bad": pixels flagged by any of NaN, bad flux, fibre status or mask, and spaxels with any pixel flagged by NaN, bad median flux, fibre status or mask.

docs.text:
The offset and scale that normalise data as (data - offset) / scale.

NaN values are ignored. The strategies give:

Strategy Offset Scale None 0 1 "max only" 0 maximum "98 only" 0 98th percentile "extrema" minimum maximum - minimum "1σ" mean 2 × standard deviation "2σ" mean 4 × standard deviation "3σ" mean 6 × standard deviation "padded" minimum - 0.15 × range 1.3 × range

docs.title: lvm_tools.LVMTile dataclass
docs.text:
One LVM exposure: its science-fibre spectra and metadata, read lazily from a DRP file.

Create one with LVMTile.from_file. The cubes are Dask arrays, so nothing is read from disk until values are computed, and selecting part of the data (for example a wavelength window) only reads that part.

Attributes:

Name Type Description data Dataset

The exposure as an xarray.Dataset.

Data variables, each of shape (1, n_spaxels, n_wavelengths) with dimensions (tile, spaxel, wavelength), held as Dask arrays:

  • flux: flux, in erg cm⁻² s⁻¹ Å⁻¹ (FLUX_UNIT).
  • i_var: inverse variance of the flux, in FLUX_UNIT**-2.
  • lsf_sigma: Gaussian standard deviation of the line spread function, in Angstrom (converted from the FWHM stored in the file).
  • mask: the DRP pixel mask; 1 marks a bad pixel.

Coordinates (NumPy arrays):

  • tile: the exposure number (length 1).
  • spaxel: spaxel index, 0 .. n_spaxels - 1.
  • wavelength: wavelength grid, in Angstrom.
  • mjd: Modified Julian Date of the exposure midpoint, along tile.
  • ra, dec: right ascension and declination of each spaxel, in degrees, shape (1, n_spaxels).
  • fibre_id: fibre identifier from the slitmap, shape (1, n_spaxels).
  • ifu_label: IFU bundle label ("Sci1", "Sci2" or "Sci3").
  • fibre_status: fibre status flag from the slitmap; 0 marks a good fibre.

The exposure's metadata.

docs.text: mask_near_points is useful for restricting a model evaluated on a grid (e.g. a map made on a grid of sky_x, sky_y) to the region covered by data, so sparse regions aren't extrapolated into.

docs.title: lvm_tools.utils.mask.mask_near_points(xgrid, ygrid, xpoints, ypoints, threshold=None)
docs.text:
A boolean mask of the points of a 2D grid that are close to at least one data point.

The nearest data point to each grid point is found with a KD-tree. Use it to restrict a model evaluated on a grid to where there are data.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default xgrid ndarray

Grid coordinates along x (monotonically increasing).

required ygrid ndarray

Grid coordinates along y (monotonically increasing).

required xpoints ndarray

x coordinates of the data points.

required ypoints ndarray

y coordinates of the data points.

required threshold float | None

A grid point is kept if its nearest data point is closer than this. If None, 1.5 times the larger of the mean grid spacings in x and y.

None

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

Boolean mask of shape (len(ygrid), len(xgrid)), True where the grid point is near a data point ("keep").

Example 
import numpy as np
from lvm_tools.utils.mask import mask_near_points

xgrid = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
ygrid = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
xpoints = np.random.uniform(2, 8, 50)
ypoints = np.random.uniform(2, 8, 50)

mask = mask_near_points(xgrid, ygrid, xpoints, ypoints)
data = np.ones((len(ygrid), len(xgrid)))
masked_data = np.where(mask, data, np.nan)

docs.title: Tutorial: Data Configuration
docs.text: This tutorial covers the DataConfig class and its options for controlling data processing.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
DataConfig is an immutable dataclass that specifies:

  1. Clipping: Wavelength and spatial ranges to include
  2. Filtering: Strategies for handling bad data
  3. Normalisation: Methods for scaling flux and coordinates

docs.title: Default Configuration
docs.text:
Create a configuration with default settings:

from lvm_tools import DataConfig

config = DataConfig.default()
print(config)

This uses the full wavelength range with standard filtering and normalisation.

docs.title: Configuration from Data
docs.text:
The recommended approach is to derive configuration from your data:

from lvm_tools import LVMTile, DataConfig
from pathlib import Path

# Load tile
tile = LVMTile.from_file(Path("/path/to/data.fits"))

# Create configuration with automatic parameter calculation
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    tile,
    λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0),  # H-alpha region
)

print(config)

The from_tiles method:

  • Sets α_range and δ_range from the tile's spatial extent
  • Calculates normalisation offsets and scales from the data
  • Applies any user-specified overrides

docs.title: Single Range
docs.text:
Select a single wavelength range:

config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    tile,
    λ_range=(4800.0, 5100.0),  # OIII region
)

docs.title: Multiple Ranges
docs.text:
Select multiple non-overlapping ranges:

config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    tile,
    λ_range=(
        (4800.0, 4900.0),  # H-beta
        (4950.0, 5050.0),  # OIII doublet
    ),
)

Ranges must be ordered and non-overlapping.

docs.title: Spatial Clipping
docs.text:
Restrict to a spatial region:

config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    tile,
    λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0),
    α_range=(180.0, 181.0),  # RA in degrees
    δ_range=(-30.0, -29.0),  # Dec in degrees
)

By default, from_tiles computes a bounding square that encompasses all data with 1% padding.

docs.title: NaN Strategy
docs.text:
Control how NaN values are handled:

# Exclude individual NaN pixels (default)
config = DataConfig(
    nans_strategy="pixel",
    # ... other parameters
)

# Exclude entire spaxels containing any NaN
config = DataConfig(
    nans_strategy="spaxel",
    # ... other parameters
)

docs.title: Bad Flux Strategy
docs.text:
Control how bad flux values are identified:

# Per-pixel threshold (strict)
config = DataConfig(
    F_bad_strategy="pixel",
    F_range=(-1e-14, 1e-10),
    # ...
)

# Per-spaxel median threshold (tolerant)
config = DataConfig(
    F_bad_strategy="spaxel",
    F_range=(-1e-14, 1e-10),
    # ...
)

# Per-spaxel maximum threshold
config = DataConfig(
    F_bad_strategy="spaxel_max",
    F_range=(-1e-14, 1e-10),
    # ...
)

The default F_range lower bound is -0.1e-13, designed to exclude unphysical negative fluxes.

docs.title: Fibre Status Filtering
docs.text:
Include only specific fibre status values:

# Include only status 0 (default - good fibres)
config = DataConfig(
    fibre_status_include=(0,),
    # ...
)

# Include multiple status values
config = DataConfig(
    fibre_status_include=(0, 1),
    # ...
)

docs.title: DRP Mask
docs.text:
Control whether to apply the DRP quality mask:

# Apply mask (default)
config = DataConfig(
    apply_mask=True,
    # ...
)

# Ignore mask
config = DataConfig(
    apply_mask=False,
    # ...
)

docs.title: Flux Normalisation
docs.text:
Several strategies are available for normalising flux:

# No normalisation
config = DataConfig(normalise_F_strategy=None)

# Divide by maximum (default)
config = DataConfig(normalise_F_strategy="max only")

# Divide by 98th percentile (robust to outliers)
config = DataConfig(normalise_F_strategy="98 only")

# Shift to minimum, scale by range
config = DataConfig(normalise_F_strategy="extrema")

# Centre on mean, scale by the width of ±2σ (4 standard deviations)
config = DataConfig(normalise_F_strategy="2σ")

# Shift and scale to the data range, with 15% padding on each side
config = DataConfig(normalise_F_strategy="padded")

docs.title: Coordinate Normalisation
docs.text:
The same strategies apply to RA/Dec coordinates:

config = DataConfig(
    normalise_αδ_strategy="padded",  # Default
    # ...
)

The padded strategy is recommended for coordinates as it ensures the domain has a small buffer.

docs.title: Manual Normalisation Parameters
docs.text:
Override calculated normalisation parameters:

config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    tile,
    λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0),
    normalise_F_offset=0.0,
    normalise_F_scale=1e-14,
    normalise_α_offset=180.0,
    normalise_α_scale=1.0,
    normalise_δ_offset=-30.0,
    normalise_δ_scale=1.0,
)

docs.title: Convert to/from Dictionary
docs.text:
# To dictionary
config_dict = config.to_dict()
print(config_dict)

# From dictionary
restored = DataConfig.from_dict(config_dict)

This enables saving configurations to JSON or YAML.

docs.title: Configuration Validation
docs.text:
All parameters are validated on instantiation:

# Invalid range (max < min)
try:
    config = DataConfig(
        λ_range=(6800.0, 6500.0),  # Invalid!
        # ...
    )
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Validation error: {e}")

# Invalid strategy
try:
    config = DataConfig(
        nans_strategy="invalid_strategy",  # Unknown!
        # ...
    )
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Validation error: {e}")

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
from lvm_tools import LVMTile, DataConfig

# Load data
tile = LVMTile.from_file(Path("/path/to/data.fits"))

# Create a comprehensive configuration
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    tiles=tile,
    # Wavelength selection
    λ_range=(
        (4800.0, 4880.0),  # H-beta
        (4940.0, 5040.0),  # OIII
        (6540.0, 6600.0),  # H-alpha + NII
    ),
    # Filtering
    nans_strategy="pixel",
    F_bad_strategy="spaxel",
    F_range=(-1e-14, np.inf),
    fibre_status_include=(0,),
    apply_mask=True,
    # Normalisation
    normalise_F_strategy="98 only",
    normalise_αδ_strategy="padded",
)

print(config)

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use from_tiles when possible to automatically calculate normalisation parameters.
  2. Start with defaults and adjust parameters incrementally.
  3. Document your configuration by saving the dictionary representation.
  4. Use the hash for tracking which configuration produced which results.

docs.title: Tutorial: Exploring LVM Data
docs.text: This tutorial demonstrates how to explore and visualise LVM data, including spatial distributions and spectral properties.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This tutorial assumes you have completed Tutorial: Loading LVM Data and have access to LVM DRP files. We will use matplotlib for visualisation:

pip install matplotlib

docs.title: Loading the Data
docs.text:
Begin by loading a tile:

from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from lvm_tools import LVMTile

# Load a tile
tile = LVMTile.from_file(Path("/path/to/lvm-drp-observation.fits"))

# Extract the dataset for convenience
ds = tile.data

print(tile)

docs.title: Plotting Sky Positions
docs.text:
Visualise the spatial distribution of fibres on the sky:

# Extract coordinates
ra = ds["ra"].values.flatten()
dec = ds["dec"].values.flatten()

# Create a scatter plot of fibre positions
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))

scatter = ax.scatter(ra, dec, c=np.arange(len(ra)), cmap="viridis", s=10)
ax.set_xlabel("Right Ascension (deg)")
ax.set_ylabel("Declination (deg)")
ax.set_title("LVM Fibre Positions")
ax.set_aspect("equal")

# Invert RA axis (standard astronomical convention)
ax.invert_xaxis()

plt.colorbar(scatter, ax=ax, label="Fibre index")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Colour-Coding by IFU Bundle
docs.text:
LVM uses three science IFU bundles. Visualise their spatial arrangement:

# Get IFU labels
ifu_labels = ds["ifu_label"].values.flatten()
unique_ifus = np.unique(ifu_labels)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))

colors = {"Sci1": "C0", "Sci2": "C1", "Sci3": "C2"}
for ifu in unique_ifus:
    mask = ifu_labels == ifu
    ax.scatter(ra[mask], dec[mask], c=colors.get(ifu, "gray"), label=ifu, s=15, alpha=0.7)

ax.set_xlabel("Right Ascension (deg)")
ax.set_ylabel("Declination (deg)")
ax.set_title("LVM IFU Bundle Positions")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.invert_xaxis()
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Colour-Coding by Fibre Status
docs.text:
Identify fibres with different quality flags:

# Get fibre status
fibre_status = ds["fibre_status"].values.flatten()
unique_status = np.unique(fibre_status)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))

status_colors = {0: "green", 1: "orange", 2: "red", 3: "gray"}
status_labels = {0: "Good", 1: "Warning", 2: "Bad", 3: "Unknown"}

for status in unique_status:
    mask = fibre_status == status
    ax.scatter(
        ra[mask],
        dec[mask],
        c=status_colors.get(status, "black"),
        label=f"Status {status} ({status_labels.get(status, 'Unknown')})",
        s=15,
        alpha=0.7,
    )

ax.set_xlabel("Right Ascension (deg)")
ax.set_ylabel("Declination (deg)")
ax.set_title("Fibre Status Distribution")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.invert_xaxis()
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Plotting Individual Spectra
docs.text:
Extract and plot spectra from individual spaxels:

# Get wavelength grid
wavelength = ds["wavelength"].values

# Select a spaxel index
spaxel_idx = 100

# Extract flux and inverse variance (compute from Dask)
flux = ds["flux"].isel(tile=0, spaxel=spaxel_idx).values
ivar = ds["i_var"].isel(tile=0, spaxel=spaxel_idx).values

# Compute uncertainty (standard deviation)
sigma = np.where(ivar > 0, 1.0 / np.sqrt(ivar), np.nan)

# Get position of this spaxel
spaxel_ra = float(ds["ra"].isel(tile=0, spaxel=spaxel_idx))
spaxel_dec = float(ds["dec"].isel(tile=0, spaxel=spaxel_idx))

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4))

ax.plot(wavelength, flux, "k-", lw=0.5, label="Flux")
ax.fill_between(
    wavelength, flux - sigma, flux + sigma, alpha=0.3, color="C0", label=r"$\pm 1\sigma$"
)

ax.set_xlabel(r"Wavelength ($\mathrm{\AA}$)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"Flux (erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ $\mathrm{\AA}^{-1}$)")
ax.set_title(f"Spectrum at RA={spaxel_ra:.4f}, Dec={spaxel_dec:.4f}")
ax.legend()
ax.set_xlim(wavelength.min(), wavelength.max())
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Zooming into Spectral Features
docs.text:
Examine specific wavelength regions:

# Define wavelength regions of interest
regions = {
    r"H$\beta$ + [OIII]": (4800, 5100),
    r"H$\alpha$ + [NII]": (6500, 6650),
    r"[SII] doublet": (6700, 6750),
}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))

for ax, (name, (wl_min, wl_max)) in zip(axes, regions.items()):
    # Select wavelength range
    mask = (wavelength >= wl_min) & (wavelength <= wl_max)
    wl_subset = wavelength[mask]
    flux_subset = flux[mask]
    sigma_subset = sigma[mask]

    ax.plot(wl_subset, flux_subset, "k-", lw=0.8)
    ax.fill_between(
        wl_subset, flux_subset - sigma_subset, flux_subset + sigma_subset, alpha=0.3, color="C0"
    )

    ax.set_xlabel(r"Wavelength ($\mathrm{\AA}$)")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"Flux")
    ax.set_title(name)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Plotting Multiple Spectra
docs.text:
Compare spectra from different spatial locations:

# Select multiple spaxels
spaxel_indices = [50, 100, 150, 200, 250]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 6))

for i, idx in enumerate(spaxel_indices):
    flux_i = ds["flux"].isel(tile=0, spaxel=idx).values
    ra_i = float(ds["ra"].isel(tile=0, spaxel=idx))
    dec_i = float(ds["dec"].isel(tile=0, spaxel=idx))

    # Offset for visibility
    offset = i * 1e-15
    ax.plot(wavelength, flux_i + offset, lw=0.5, label=f"({ra_i:.3f}, {dec_i:.3f})")

ax.set_xlabel(r"Wavelength ($\mathrm{\AA}$)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"Flux + offset")
ax.set_title("Spectra from Multiple Positions")
ax.legend(title="(RA, Dec)", fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(wavelength.min(), wavelength.max())
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Spatial Maps of Spectral Properties
docs.text:
Create maps of integrated flux in specific wavelength windows:

# Define a wavelength window around H-alpha
ha_min, ha_max = 6555.0, 6575.0
wl_mask = (wavelength >= ha_min) & (wavelength <= ha_max)

# Compute integrated flux for all spaxels
# Note: this triggers Dask computation
flux_cube = ds["flux"].isel(tile=0).values  # Shape: (n_spaxels, n_wavelengths)
ha_flux = np.nansum(flux_cube[:, wl_mask], axis=1)

# Plot spatial map
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))

scatter = ax.scatter(
    ra,
    dec,
    c=ha_flux,
    cmap="plasma",
    s=20,
    vmin=np.nanpercentile(ha_flux, 5),
    vmax=np.nanpercentile(ha_flux, 95),
)

ax.set_xlabel("Right Ascension (deg)")
ax.set_ylabel("Declination (deg)")
ax.set_title(r"H$\alpha$ Integrated Flux Map")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.invert_xaxis()

plt.colorbar(scatter, ax=ax, label=r"Flux (erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Continuum-Subtracted Maps
docs.text:
Create maps with local continuum subtraction:

# Define continuum windows on either side of H-alpha
cont_blue = (6500.0, 6540.0)
cont_red = (6590.0, 6630.0)

# Masks for each window
blue_mask = (wavelength >= cont_blue[0]) & (wavelength <= cont_blue[1])
red_mask = (wavelength >= cont_red[0]) & (wavelength <= cont_red[1])

# Compute median continuum
cont_blue_flux = np.nanmedian(flux_cube[:, blue_mask], axis=1)
cont_red_flux = np.nanmedian(flux_cube[:, red_mask], axis=1)
continuum = 0.5 * (cont_blue_flux + cont_red_flux)

# Subtract continuum from H-alpha flux
ha_flux_cont_sub = ha_flux - continuum * np.sum(wl_mask)

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 6))

# Raw H-alpha flux
sc1 = axes[0].scatter(
    ra,
    dec,
    c=ha_flux,
    cmap="plasma",
    s=20,
    vmin=np.nanpercentile(ha_flux, 5),
    vmax=np.nanpercentile(ha_flux, 95),
)
axes[0].set_title(r"H$\alpha$ (raw)")
plt.colorbar(sc1, ax=axes[0])

# Continuum-subtracted
sc2 = axes[1].scatter(
    ra,
    dec,
    c=ha_flux_cont_sub,
    cmap="RdBu_r",
    s=20,
    vmin=np.nanpercentile(ha_flux_cont_sub, 5),
    vmax=np.nanpercentile(ha_flux_cont_sub, 95),
)
axes[1].set_title(r"H$\alpha$ (continuum subtracted)")
plt.colorbar(sc2, ax=axes[1])

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("Right Ascension (deg)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Declination (deg)")
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.invert_xaxis()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Signal-to-Noise Maps
docs.text:
Visualise data quality across the field:

# Compute median S/N per spaxel
ivar_cube = ds["i_var"].isel(tile=0).values
sigma_cube = np.where(ivar_cube > 0, 1.0 / np.sqrt(ivar_cube), np.nan)
snr_cube = flux_cube / sigma_cube

# Median S/N across wavelength
median_snr = np.nanmedian(snr_cube, axis=1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))

scatter = ax.scatter(
    ra, dec, c=median_snr, cmap="viridis", s=20, vmin=0, vmax=np.nanpercentile(median_snr, 95)
)

ax.set_xlabel("Right Ascension (deg)")
ax.set_ylabel("Declination (deg)")
ax.set_title("Median Signal-to-Noise Ratio")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.invert_xaxis()

plt.colorbar(scatter, ax=ax, label="Median S/N per pixel")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Line Spread Function Visualisation
docs.text:
Examine the spectral resolution across the field:

# Get LSF sigma (already converted from FWHM)
lsf_cube = ds["lsf_sigma"].isel(tile=0).values

# Median LSF at a reference wavelength (e.g., H-alpha)
ha_wl_idx = np.argmin(np.abs(wavelength - 6563.0))
lsf_at_ha = lsf_cube[:, ha_wl_idx]

# Convert sigma to FWHM for display
SIGMA_TO_FWHM = 2.355
lsf_fwhm = lsf_at_ha * SIGMA_TO_FWHM

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 8))

scatter = ax.scatter(ra, dec, c=lsf_fwhm, cmap="coolwarm", s=20)

ax.set_xlabel("Right Ascension (deg)")
ax.set_ylabel("Declination (deg)")
ax.set_title(r"LSF FWHM at H$\alpha$ ($\mathrm{\AA}$)")
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.invert_xaxis()

plt.colorbar(scatter, ax=ax, label=r"FWHM ($\mathrm{\AA}$)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Summary Statistics
docs.text:
Generate summary statistics for the observation:

# Compute various statistics
n_spaxels = len(ra)
n_wavelengths = len(wavelength)
n_good_fibres = np.sum(fibre_status == 0)

# Wavelength coverage
wl_min, wl_max = wavelength.min(), wavelength.max()
wl_step = np.median(np.diff(wavelength))

# Spatial coverage
ra_range = ra.max() - ra.min()
dec_range = dec.max() - dec.min()

# Data quality
valid_fraction = np.mean(~np.isnan(flux_cube))
median_snr_all = np.nanmedian(snr_cube)

print("=" * 50)
print("LVM Observation Summary")
print("=" * 50)
print(f"Tile ID:           {tile.meta.tile_id}")
print(f"Exposure:          {tile.meta.exp_num}")
print(f"DRP Version:       {tile.meta.drp_ver}")
print("-" * 50)
print(f"Spaxels:           {n_spaxels}")
print(f"Good fibres:       {n_good_fibres} ({100 * n_good_fibres / n_spaxels:.1f}%)")
print(f"Wavelength points: {n_wavelengths}")
print(f"Wavelength range:  {wl_min:.1f} - {wl_max:.1f} Å")
print(f"Wavelength step:   {wl_step:.3f} Å")
print("-" * 50)
print(f"RA range:          {ra.min():.4f} - {ra.max():.4f} deg ({ra_range * 60:.2f} arcmin)")
print(f"Dec range:         {dec.min():.4f} - {dec.max():.4f} deg ({dec_range * 60:.2f} arcmin)")
print("-" * 50)
print(f"Valid data:        {100 * valid_fraction:.1f}%")
print(f"Median S/N:        {median_snr_all:.1f}")
print("=" * 50)

docs.title: Tutorial: Model Fitting Workflow
docs.text: This tutorial demonstrates a complete workflow from data loading to model-ready arrays.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The typical lvm_tools workflow consists of:

  1. Load raw data from FITS files
  2. Configure data processing parameters
  3. Build normalised arrays for fitting
  4. Access data properties for model construction

This tutorial covers each step in detail.

docs.title: Step 1: Load Data
docs.text:
Begin by loading one or more tiles:

from pathlib import Path
from lvm_tools import LVMTile, LVMTileCollection

# Single tile
tile = LVMTile.from_file(Path("/path/to/observation.fits"))

# Multiple tiles (e.g., dithered observations)
paths = list(Path("/path/to/data/").glob("*.fits"))
tiles = [LVMTile.from_file(p) for p in sorted(paths)]
collection = LVMTileCollection.from_tiles(tiles)

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Processing
docs.text:
Create a DataConfig that matches your analysis requirements:

from lvm_tools import DataConfig

# For emission line analysis
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    collection,
    λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0),  # H-alpha region
    nans_strategy="pixel",
    F_bad_strategy="spaxel",
    normalise_F_strategy="98 only",
)

# Inspect the configuration
print(config)

docs.title: Step 3: Build FitData
docs.text:
Combine tiles and configuration to produce fit-ready data:

from lvm_tools import FitDataBuilder

# Create builder
builder = FitDataBuilder(tiles=collection, config=config)

# Build the data (triggers Dask computation)
fit_data = builder.build()

# Record the pipeline hash for reproducibility
pipeline_hash = builder.hash()
print(f"Pipeline: {pipeline_hash[:16]}...")

docs.title: Step 4: Access Data Arrays
docs.text: FitData provides normalised JAX arrays:

docs.title: Spectral Data
docs.text:
# Normalised flux (NaN replaced with 0)
flux = fit_data.flux
print(f"Flux shape: {flux.shape}")

# Inverse variance (NaN replaced with small value)
ivar = fit_data.i_var

# Uncertainty (standard deviation)
sigma = fit_data.u_flux

# Wavelength grid
wavelength = fit_data.λ
print(f"Wavelength range: {float(wavelength.min()):.1f} - {float(wavelength.max()):.1f} Å")

# Line spread function
lsf = fit_data.lsf_σ

docs.title: Spatial Data
docs.text:
# Normalised coordinates (mapped to [-π, π])
alpha = fit_data.α  # Right ascension
delta = fit_data.δ  # Declination

print(f"Number of spaxels: {len(alpha)}")

# Convert back to physical coordinates
ra_physical = fit_data.predict_α(alpha)
dec_physical = fit_data.predict_δ(delta)

docs.title: Masking
docs.text:
# Boolean mask (True where data is valid)
mask = fit_data.mask
print(f"Valid pixels: {float(mask.sum())} / {mask.size}")

# Apply mask in computations
masked_flux = flux * mask

docs.title: Indexing
docs.text:
# Wavelength indices
λ_idx = fit_data.λ_idx

# Spaxel indices
spaxel_idx = fit_data.spaxel_idx

# Tile indices (for multi-tile data)
tile_idx = fit_data.tile_idx

# IFU bundle indices
ifu_idx = fit_data.ifu_idx

# Fibre indices
fibre_idx = fit_data.fibre_idx

docs.title: Physical Properties
docs.text:
# Observation time
mjd = fit_data.mjd
print(f"MJD: {float(mjd.mean()):.4f}")

# Barycentric velocity correction
v_bary = fit_data.v_bary
print(f"v_bary range: {float(v_bary.min()):.2f} - {float(v_bary.max()):.2f} km/s")

docs.title: Using with JAX Models
docs.text:
The arrays are ready for JAX-based model fitting:

import jax.numpy as jnp

# Example: compute mean spectrum
mean_spectrum = jnp.nanmean(fit_data.flux, axis=0)

# Example: compute spatial weighted mean
weights = fit_data.mask.astype(jnp.float32)
weighted_mean = jnp.sum(fit_data.flux * weights, axis=0) / jnp.sum(weights, axis=0)

docs.title: Using with spectracles
docs.text:
When spectracles is installed, sky_data gives the spaxel positions in arcseconds, east and north of the field's centre. Fields then take length scales in arcseconds:

from spectracles import Domain, FourierGP, Matern32, Parameter
from spectracles.priors import LogNormal

spaxels = fit_data.sky_data
domain = Domain.from_points(spaxels.x, spaxels.y)
kernel = Matern32(
    length_scale=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(60.0, 20.0)),  # arcsec
    variance=Parameter(prior=LogNormal(1.0, 0.5)),
)
flux = FourierGP(kernel, domain=domain)

# A map on a grid, back in RA and Dec
ra, dec = fit_data.sky_to_radec(grid_x, grid_y)

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
The FitDataBuilder.hash() method generates a unique identifier:

import json

# Generate hash
pipeline_hash = builder.hash()

# Save configuration for reproducibility
metadata = {
    "hash": pipeline_hash,
    "config": config.to_dict(),
    "n_tiles": len(collection.meta),
    "exposures": list(collection.meta.keys()),
}

with open("pipeline_metadata.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(metadata, f, indent=2, default=str)

docs.title: Memory Management
docs.text:
For large datasets, manage memory carefully:

import gc

# Process in batches
batch_size = 100
for i in range(0, len(paths), batch_size):
    batch_paths = paths[i : i + batch_size]
    batch_tiles = [LVMTile.from_file(p) for p in batch_paths]
    batch_collection = LVMTileCollection.from_tiles(batch_tiles)

    # Configure and build
    config = DataConfig.from_tiles(batch_collection, λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0))
    fit_data = FitDataBuilder(batch_collection, config).build()

    # Process this batch
    # ...

    # Clean up
    del batch_tiles, batch_collection, fit_data
    gc.collect()

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
import json
from lvm_tools import LVMTile, LVMTileCollection, DataConfig, FitDataBuilder

# 1. Load data
data_dir = Path("/path/to/lvm/data/")
paths = sorted(data_dir.glob("lvm-drp-*.fits"))
tiles = [LVMTile.from_file(p) for p in paths]
collection = LVMTileCollection.from_tiles(tiles)

print(f"Loaded {len(tiles)} tiles")
print(collection)

# 2. Configure processing
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    collection,
    λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0),
    nans_strategy="pixel",
    F_bad_strategy="spaxel",
    fibre_status_include=(0,),
    apply_mask=True,
    normalise_F_strategy="98 only",
    normalise_αδ_strategy="padded",
)

print("\nConfiguration:")
print(config)

# 3. Build fit data
builder = FitDataBuilder(tiles=collection, config=config)
fit_data = builder.build()

print(f"\nFit data built successfully")
print(f"  Flux shape: {fit_data.flux.shape}")
print(f"  Wavelength points: {len(fit_data.λ)}")
print(f"  Spaxels: {len(fit_data.α)}")

# 4. Save metadata
metadata = {
    "pipeline_hash": builder.hash(),
    "config": config.to_dict(),
    "n_tiles": len(collection.meta),
    "flux_shape": list(fit_data.flux.shape),
}

with open("analysis_metadata.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(metadata, f, indent=2, default=str)

# 5. Ready for model fitting
# ... your analysis code here ...

docs.title: Tutorial: Loading LVM Data
docs.text: This tutorial provides a comprehensive guide to loading and inspecting LVM DRP data using lvm_tools.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Ensure you have lvm_tools installed and access to LVM DRP FITS files. The examples assume familiarity with Python and basic astronomical data concepts.

docs.title: LVM DRP File Structure
docs.text:
LVM DRP output files are multi-extension FITS files containing:

  • HDU 0: Primary header with observation metadata
  • HDU 1: Flux cube (science fibre spectra)
  • HDU 2: Inverse variance cube
  • HDU 3: Data quality mask
  • HDU 4: Wavelength solution
  • HDU 5: Line spread function (FWHM)
  • HDU -1: Slitmap (fibre positions and metadata)

docs.title: Loading a Single Tile
docs.text:
The LVMTile class handles all FITS parsing:

from pathlib import Path
from lvm_tools import LVMTile

# Define the path to your DRP file
drp_path = Path("/path/to/lvm-drp-0012345-00001.fits")

# Load the tile
tile = LVMTile.from_file(drp_path)

# Display tile information
print(tile)

Output:

LVMTile (0x7f...):
    Filename:        lvm-drp-0012345-00001.fits
    Exposure:        1
    DRP version:     1.0.0
    Tile ID:         12345
    Data size:        156MB
    Dimensions:       tile: 1, spaxel: 1801, wavelength: 7676
    Coordinates:
        wavelength    (wavelength)                 float64  60kB   [Angstrom]
        ra            (tile, spaxel)               float64  14kB   [deg]
        dec           (tile, spaxel)               float64  14kB   [deg]
        ...
    Data:
        flux          (tile, spaxel, wavelength)   float64  105MB  DaskArray [erg / (Angstrom cm2 s)]
        i_var         (tile, spaxel, wavelength)   float64  105MB  DaskArray [1 / erg2 / (Angstrom2 cm4 s2)]
        ...

docs.title: Accessing Tile Data
docs.text:
The underlying data is stored in an xarray Dataset:

# Access the Dataset
ds = tile.data

# List all variables
print("Data variables:", list(ds.data_vars))
print("Coordinates:", list(ds.coords))

# Access specific arrays
flux = ds["flux"]
wavelength = ds["wavelength"]

print(f"Flux shape: {flux.shape}")
print(f"Wavelength range: {float(wavelength.min()):.1f} - {float(wavelength.max()):.1f} Å")

docs.title: Lazy Evaluation with Dask
docs.text:
Flux, inverse variance, mask, and LSF arrays are Dask arrays, loaded lazily:

# Check if data is lazily loaded
print(f"Flux chunks: {tile.data['flux'].data.chunks}")

# Compute a subset without loading everything
subset = tile.data["flux"].isel(spaxel=slice(0, 10))

# Trigger computation
subset_values = subset.values  # or subset.compute()
print(f"Subset shape: {subset_values.shape}")

Coordinates are eagerly loaded as they are typically small.

docs.title: Accessing Metadata
docs.text:
Tile metadata is stored in the meta attribute:

# Access metadata
print(f"Filename: {tile.meta.filename}")
print(f"Tile ID: {tile.meta.tile_id}")
print(f"Exposure number: {tile.meta.exp_num}")
print(f"DRP version: {tile.meta.drp_ver}")

docs.title: Loading Multiple Tiles
docs.text:
For multi-exposure analyses, combine tiles into a collection:

from lvm_tools import LVMTile, LVMTileCollection

# Load multiple tiles
paths = [
    Path("/path/to/exposure_1.fits"),
    Path("/path/to/exposure_2.fits"),
    Path("/path/to/exposure_3.fits"),
]
tiles = [LVMTile.from_file(p) for p in paths]

# Create a collection
collection = LVMTileCollection.from_tiles(tiles)

# Inspect the collection
print(collection)

The collection concatenates data along the tile dimension:

# Access combined data
print(f"Number of tiles: {len(collection.meta)}")
print(f"Combined flux shape: {collection.data['flux'].shape}")

# Metadata is accessible by exposure number
for exp_num, meta in collection.meta.items():
    print(f"Exposure {exp_num}: {meta.filename}")

docs.title: Working with Coordinates
docs.text:
Spatial coordinates (RA, Dec) are stored per spaxel:

import numpy as np

# Access coordinates
ra = tile.data["ra"].values.flatten()
dec = tile.data["dec"].values.flatten()

# Compute field centre
ra_centre = np.mean(ra)
dec_centre = np.mean(dec)
print(f"Field centre: ({ra_centre:.4f}, {dec_centre:.4f}) deg")

# Compute field extent
print(f"RA range: {ra.min():.4f} - {ra.max():.4f} deg")
print(f"Dec range: {dec.min():.4f} - {dec.max():.4f} deg")

docs.title: Fibre Information
docs.text:
Fibre-level metadata is available for quality filtering:

# Fibre status flags
fibre_status = tile.data["fibre_status"].values.flatten()
unique_status = np.unique(fibre_status)
print(f"Fibre status values: {unique_status}")

# Count by status
for status in unique_status:
    count = np.sum(fibre_status == status)
    print(f"  Status {status}: {count} fibres")

# IFU labels
ifu_labels = tile.data["ifu_label"].values.flatten()
unique_ifu = np.unique(ifu_labels)
print(f"IFU bundles: {unique_ifu}")

docs.title: Wavelength Grid
docs.text:
The wavelength solution is common to all spaxels:

# Access wavelength grid
wavelength = tile.data["wavelength"].values
print(f"Wavelength points: {len(wavelength)}")
print(f"Range: {wavelength.min():.1f} - {wavelength.max():.1f} Å")

# Compute spectral resolution
delta_lambda = np.diff(wavelength)
print(f"Pixel size: {delta_lambda.mean():.3f} Å (mean)")

docs.title: Line Spread Function
docs.text:
The LSF is provided as sigma (converted from FWHM in the DRP):

# LSF sigma array
lsf_sigma = tile.data["lsf_sigma"]
print(f"LSF shape: {lsf_sigma.shape}")

# Median LSF over fibres at one wavelength pixel
lsf_at_pixel = lsf_sigma.isel(wavelength=3000)
median_lsf = float(np.nanmedian(lsf_at_pixel.values))
λ_pixel = float(lsf_at_pixel["wavelength"])
print(f"Median LSF sigma at {λ_pixel:.1f} Å: {median_lsf:.2f} Å")

docs.title: Observation Time
docs.text:
The Modified Julian Date (MJD) is computed from the observation midpoint:

# Access MJD
mjd = tile.data["mjd"].values
print(f"Observation MJD: {mjd[0]:.6f}")

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Handle missing or corrupted files gracefully:

from pathlib import Path
from lvm_tools import LVMTile

path = Path("/path/to/nonexistent.fits")

try:
    tile = LVMTile.from_file(path)
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"File not found: {path}")

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: This section describes the design philosophy and key abstractions in lvm_tools.

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
lvm_tools is built around three core principles:

  1. Lazy evaluation: Data is loaded on-demand using Dask, minimising memory footprint for large datasets.
  2. Modularity: Each processing step (clipping, filtering, normalisation) is independent and composable.
  3. Reproducibility: Configurations are immutable dataclasses that can be hashed and serialised.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
The typical data flow in lvm_tools follows this pattern:

FITS File(s)
     │
     ▼
LVMTile / LVMTileCollection    ─────────────────────────────────────┐
     │                                                               │
     │  (lazy xarray Dataset with Dask arrays)                      │
     ▼                                                               │
DataConfig.from_tiles()        ←── λ_range, filtering options       │
     │                                                               │
     │  (calculates normalisation parameters)                       │
     ▼                                                               │
FitDataBuilder(tiles, config)                                       │
     │                                                               │
     │  .build()                                                    │
     ▼                                                               │
FitData                        ─────────────────────────────────────┘
     │
     │  (normalised JAX arrays ready for fitting)
     ▼
Model Fitting (e.g., spectracles)

docs.title: LVMTile and LVMTileCollection
docs.text:
LVMTile represents a single LVM observation, containing:

  • Flux cube: 2D array of shape (n_spaxels, n_wavelengths)
  • Inverse variance: Corresponding uncertainty estimates
  • Mask: Data quality flags from the DRP
  • LSF sigma: Line spread function width at each pixel
  • Coordinates: Wavelength grid, RA/Dec positions, fibre metadata

Data is stored in an xarray Dataset with Dask-backed arrays for memory efficiency:

tile = LVMTile.from_file(path)

# Access the underlying Dataset
ds = tile.data

# Data variables (Dask arrays)
ds["flux"]  # Shape: (1, n_spaxels, n_wavelengths)
ds["i_var"]  # Inverse variance
ds["lsf_sigma"]  # Line spread function (sigma, not FWHM)
ds["mask"]  # DRP quality mask

# Coordinates
ds["wavelength"]  # Wavelength grid (Angstroms)
ds["ra"]  # Right ascension (degrees)
ds["dec"]  # Declination (degrees)
ds["fibre_status"]  # Fibre quality flags

LVMTileCollection concatenates multiple tiles along the tile dimension, enabling multi-exposure analyses.

docs.title: DataConfig
docs.text: DataConfig is an immutable dataclass specifying all data processing parameters:

docs.title: Clipping Parameters
docs.text:
• λ_range: Wavelength range(s) to include. Can be a single tuple (min, max) or multiple ranges ((min1, max1), (min2, max2)).
  • α_range: Right ascension range in degrees.
  • δ_range: Declination range in degrees.

docs.title: Filtering Parameters
docs.text:
• nans_strategy: How to handle NaN values.
  • "pixel": Exclude individual NaN pixels (default)
  • "spaxel": Exclude entire spaxels containing any NaN
  • F_bad_strategy: How to identify bad flux values.
  • "pixel": Apply flux threshold per pixel
  • "spaxel": Apply threshold to median flux per spaxel
  • "spaxel_max": Apply threshold to maximum flux per spaxel
  • F_range: Valid flux range (min, max).
  • fibre_status_include: Tuple of acceptable fibre status values.
  • apply_mask: Whether to apply the DRP mask.

docs.title: Normalisation Parameters
docs.text:
• normalise_F_strategy: Flux normalisation method.
  • None: No normalisation
  • "max only": Divide by maximum value
  • "98 only": Divide by 98th percentile
  • "extrema": Shift to minimum, scale by range
  • "1σ", "2σ", "3σ": Centre on the mean, scale by the full width of ±Nσ (2N standard deviations)
  • "padded": Shift and scale to the data range, padded by 15% of the range on each side
  • normalise_αδ_strategy: Coordinate normalisation (same options).

The from_tiles class method automatically calculates normalisation offsets and scales based on the data.

docs.title: FitDataBuilder
docs.text:
FitDataBuilder combines tiles and configuration to produce fit-ready data. It provides:

  • Deterministic processing: Same inputs always produce the same outputs.
  • Hash generation: Unique identifier for each processing configuration.
builder = FitDataBuilder(tiles=tile, config=config)

# Build the data
fit_data = builder.build()

# Generate reproducibility hash
hash_value = builder.hash()

docs.title: FitData
docs.text: FitData provides normalised, JAX-compatible arrays for model fitting:

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• flux: Normalised flux array (NaN replaced with 0)
  • i_var: Normalised inverse variance (NaN replaced with small value)
  • u_flux: Uncertainty (inverse square root of variance)
  • λ: Wavelength grid
  • α: Normalised right ascension (mapped to [-π, π])
  • δ: Normalised declination (mapped to [-π, π])
  • lsf_σ: Line spread function sigma
  • mask: Boolean mask (True where data is valid)
  • mjd: Modified Julian Date
  • v_bary: Barycentric velocity correction

docs.title: Index Properties
docs.text:
• λ_idx: Wavelength indices
  • spaxel_idx: Spaxel indices
  • tile_idx: Tile indices (for multi-tile data)
  • ifu_idx: IFU indices
  • fibre_idx: Fibre indices

docs.title: Coordinate Transformations
docs.text:
The predict_α and predict_δ methods convert normalised coordinates back to physical units:

# Get physical RA from normalised coordinate
ra_physical = fit_data.predict_α(fit_data.α)

docs.title: spectracles Integration
docs.text:
When spectracles is installed, sky_data gives the spaxel positions as a SpatialDataLVM for spectrospatial models, in arcseconds: each spaxel's offset east (x) and north (y) of sky_centre, on the tangent plane. Length scales of spectracles fields are then in arcseconds too:

from spectracles import Domain

spaxels = fit_data.sky_data
domain = Domain.from_points(spaxels.x, spaxels.y)

sky_to_radec(x, y) converts offsets back to RA and Dec, and with_sky_origin(ra, dec) measures them from a centre of your choice.

The older αδ_data gives the normalised coordinates in [-π, π] instead (used with spectracles fields that have no domain).

docs.title: Physical Constants
docs.text:
lvm_tools defines several physical constants and units:

  • FLUX_UNIT: erg cm⁻² s⁻¹ Å⁻¹
  • SPECTRAL_UNIT: Angstrom
  • SPATIAL_UNIT: degree
  • SIGMA_TO_FWHM: 2√(2 ln 2) ≈ 2.355
  • FWHM_TO_SIGMA: 1 / SIGMA_TO_FWHM

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: This section describes the various methods for installing lvm_tools and its dependencies.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
lvm_tools requires Python 3.10 or later. The package has the following core dependencies:

  • astropy (>=6.0.0): Astronomical data handling and FITS I/O
  • dask (>=2024.1.0): Lazy array operations
  • jax (>=0.4.31): Accelerated numerical computing
  • numpy (>=2.0.0): Numerical array operations
  • scipy (>=1.11.0): Scientific computing utilities
  • xarray (>=2024.1.0): Labelled multi-dimensional arrays

docs.title: Installation from PyPI
docs.text:
The simplest installation method is via PyPI using pip:

pip install lvm-tools

docs.title: Using uv (Recommended)
docs.text:
For faster, more reliable dependency resolution, we recommend using uv:

uv add lvm-tools

docs.title: Installation from Source
docs.text:
For development or to access the latest features, install from source:

git clone git@github.com:TomHilder/lvm_tools.git
cd lvm_tools
pip install -e .

This creates an editable installation, allowing changes to the source code to take effect immediately.

docs.title: spectracles Integration
docs.text:
For use with the spectracles spectrospatial modelling package:

pip install lvm-tools[spectracles]

spectracles needs Python 3.11 or later, so on Python 3.10 the extra installs lvm_tools without it.

This installs the spectracles package and enables the sky_data (and αδ_data) properties on FitData objects.

docs.title: Verifying Installation
docs.text:
To verify the installation, open a Python interpreter and import the package:

import lvm_tools

print(lvm_tools.__all__)

This should output:

['DataConfig', 'FitDataBuilder', 'LVMTile', 'LVMTileCollection']

docs.title: JAX Installation Issues
docs.text: If you encounter issues with JAX installation, particularly on systems with NVIDIA GPUs, consult the JAX installation guide for platform-specific instructions.

docs.title: FITS File Access
docs.text: lvm_tools requires access to LVM DRP output files. These files are typically available through the SDSS Science Archive Server (SAS). Ensure you have appropriate access credentials and network connectivity.

docs.title: Quick Start Guide
docs.text: This guide provides a rapid introduction to the core functionality of lvm_tools. For more detailed explanations, see the Core Concepts page and the Tutorial: Loading LVM Data tutorial.

docs.title: Loading Data
docs.text:
The fundamental unit of data in lvm_tools is the LVMTile, which encapsulates a single LVM DRP observation:

from pathlib import Path
from lvm_tools import LVMTile

# Load a tile from a DRP FITS file
tile = LVMTile.from_file(Path("/path/to/lvm-drp-0012345-00001.fits"))

# Inspect the tile
print(tile)

The tile contains flux, inverse variance, wavelength, and spatial coordinates stored in an xarray Dataset with lazy Dask arrays.

docs.title: Combining Multiple Tiles
docs.text:
For analyses spanning multiple observations, combine tiles into a collection:

from lvm_tools import LVMTile, LVMTileCollection

# Load multiple tiles
tiles = [LVMTile.from_file(Path(f"/path/to/tile_{i}.fits")) for i in range(3)]

# Combine into a collection
collection = LVMTileCollection.from_tiles(tiles)

# Access combined data
print(collection.data.dims)

docs.title: Configuring Data Processing
docs.text:
The DataConfig class specifies how data should be clipped, filtered, and normalised:

from lvm_tools import DataConfig

# Create a configuration from tile data
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    tile,
    λ_range=(6500.0, 6800.0),  # Select H-alpha region
)

# Inspect the configuration
print(config)

The from_tiles method automatically calculates normalisation parameters based on the data.

docs.title: Building Fit-Ready Data
docs.text:
The FitDataBuilder combines tiles and configuration to produce data ready for model fitting:

from lvm_tools import FitDataBuilder

# Build fit data
builder = FitDataBuilder(tiles=tile, config=config)
fit_data = builder.build()

# Access normalised arrays (JAX arrays)
flux = fit_data.flux  # Shape: (n_spaxels, n_wavelengths)
wavelength = fit_data.λ  # Shape: (n_wavelengths,)
alpha = fit_data.α  # Right ascension (normalised)
delta = fit_data.δ  # Declination (normalised)

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text:
Every processing pipeline can be hashed for reproducibility:

# Generate a unique hash for this configuration
pipeline_hash = builder.hash()
print(f"Pipeline hash: {pipeline_hash[:16]}...")

This hash changes if either the input tiles or the configuration changes.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path
from lvm_tools import LVMTile, DataConfig, FitDataBuilder

# Load data
tile = LVMTile.from_file(Path("/path/to/observation.fits"))

# Configure processing
config = DataConfig.from_tiles(
    tile,
    λ_range=(4800.0, 5100.0),  # Select OIII region
    nans_strategy="pixel",  # Exclude individual NaN pixels
    normalise_F_strategy="max only",  # Normalise by maximum flux
)

# Build fit-ready data
fit_data = FitDataBuilder(tile, config).build()

# Use with JAX-based models
print(f"Flux shape: {fit_data.flux.shape}")
print(f"Wavelength range: {fit_data.λ.min():.1f} - {fit_data.λ.max():.1f} Å")
